record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: What sources produce the highly ionized environments observed in many low-metallicity and high-redshift galaxies, including nebular helium-ionizing radiation? The answer must determine whether hot Wolf-Rayet stars with comparatively weaker winds, chemically homogeneous-evolution products, Population III stars, or other massive-star channels can supply the necessary hard ionizing flux under the metallicity and evolutionary conditions of those galaxies.

evidence.quote: In parallel, signatures of highly ionized environments are also found in many low-metallicity and high-redshift galaxies. While their origin is still quite unclear, some possible sources are listed in Table 2 and will be discussed further below.

The WN3h stars and the direct WN/WO transition show that WR stars can be strong sources of He II ionizing flux throughout at least a significant part of their He-burning lifetime. This makes them very interesting sources in the context of observed nebular He II emission in lower-metallicity galaxies across a wide redshift range.

The comparison shows that in principle hot WRs with comparably weaker winds could yield the necessary hard ionizing flux. Yet, current evolution and population synthesis models essentially cannot reproduce the observed WN2 and WN3h stars, in particular as most of them do not have a companion.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Identify the astrophysical sources responsible for the highly ionized environments observed in many low-metallicity and high-redshift star-forming galaxies, in particular those producing nebular He II emission (which requires photons of energy at least 54 eV). Determine, under realistic metallicity and evolutionary conditions of such galaxies, which massive-star channels — including (i) hot Wolf-Rayet stars (e.g., WN2 and WN3h-type) with comparatively weak, optically thin winds, (ii) products of chemically homogeneous evolution, (iii) Population III stars, or (iv) other massive-star pathways — can supply the required hard ionizing flux, and assess whether stellar evolution and population-synthesis models can reproduce these populations (including the predominance of apparently single WN2/WN3h stars) so as to account for the observed nebular He II ionizing radiation.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2025) using SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper observations of SMC WN3h stars shows that hot Wolf-Rayet stars with thin winds can in principle supply enough He II ionizing photons to match observed nebular emission, and that their stellar signatures are easily diluted in unresolved spectra. However, current stellar-evolution and population-synthesis models still fail to reproduce the observed populations of single WN2/WN3h stars, and alternative channels (X-ray binaries, chemically homogeneous evolution, Pop III) remain debated. The question is therefore not yet definitively resolved.

status_evidence.title: SDSS-V LVM: Detectability of Wolf-Rayet stars and their He II ionizing flux in low-metallicity environments
status_evidence.snippet: WN3 stars with comparably thin winds produce enough photons to reproduce the observed nebular He II emission, but stellar signatures are diluted on >24 pc scales.
status_evidence.claim: WN3h stars can plausibly supply the He II ionizing flux, but their detection in unresolved low-metallicity galaxies is inherently difficult.

status_evidence.title: Can Wolf-Rayet stars be the missing ingredient to explain high-z He II ionizing radiation?
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates whether WR stars are the missing ingredient explaining high-z He II ionizing radiation.
status_evidence.claim: The origin of He II ionizing radiation in high-z galaxies remains an actively investigated open question.

status_evidence.title: A Multiwavelength Assessment Disfavoring the X-ray Binary Origin of He III Regions in Metal-Poor Star-Forming Dwarf Galaxies
status_evidence.snippet: Disfavors X-ray binaries as the dominant origin of He III regions in metal-poor dwarfs.
status_evidence.claim: Competing channels such as X-ray binaries are being ruled out, leaving the dominant source unresolved.
